title: Keeping students learning over the long holiday
description: A practical guide for Kenyan school principals on helping students keep learning during the long end-of-year break, without turning the holiday into extra school.
body:
The end-of-year break is the longest stretch students spend away from the classroom, often close to two months. Educators in many countries have documented that students lose some ground over long breaks, and that the loss tends to be larger for learners with less access to books and support at home.

The goal is not to extend school into the holiday. It is to give students light, achievable ways to stay in touch with learning, so that January starts with momentum instead of a re-start.

Why the long break matters

A student who returns in January having read little, written nothing, and practised no mathematics often needs the first weeks of term just to get back to where they ended. For Grade 10 and Grade 11 students moving into a more demanding level, that lost time is costly.

Rest is also part of healthy learning. A good holiday plan leaves room for family, chores, play, and sleep.

Holiday assignments students will actually complete

Assignments that are long, vague, and graded harshly get skipped. Those that are short, specific, and clearly linked to what comes next get done.

  • Keep the load realistic: a small number of focused tasks per subject, not a thick packet.
  • Tie tasks to the first topics of next term so that the work is a head start, not busywork.
  • Mix kinds of work: reading, short writing, practice problems, and one project-style task.
  • State plainly how the work will be used in January, for example as a diagnostic starting point.

A useful January routine: Open the term with a short, low-stakes diagnostic quiz in each subject. It shows teachers where students actually are, and it gives holiday work a clear purpose, so students see it was worth doing.

Reading beyond the textbook

A simple holiday reading programme, using books borrowed from the school library against a proper loan record, gives every student something to read. A short list of recommended titles by level makes choosing easier, and a brief reading reflection on return keeps it purposeful.

Bringing parents in

Parents are the holiday supervisors. A one-page note sent through WhatsApp or the Parent Portal, saying what is expected, how long it should take, and how parents can help, makes the plan real. Keep the tone encouraging. Parents who feel blamed for gaps stop engaging.
